tagline: A short letter from Paul to Titus on Crete about appointing faithful elders, silencing false teachers, and the good works that grace produces.
overview:
Titus is a brief letter of instruction to one of Paul's most trusted coworkers, left on the island of Crete to put the young churches there in order. Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town, men of proven character who hold firmly to sound teaching, because the churches were troubled by rebellious teachers, many from a Jewish background, who were upsetting whole households for the sake of money. He then tells Titus what to teach older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves, and why.

The why is the heart of the letter. Twice Paul grounds his practical instructions in compact summaries of the gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone and training believers to live godly lives as they wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:11-14); and when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, he saved us not because of our righteous deeds but by his mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit (3:4-7). Good works are not the root of salvation but its fruit, and the letter uses the phrase good works or good deeds again and again.

Titus is closely related to 1 Timothy in subject and vocabulary, and together with 2 Timothy it forms the group called the Pastoral Letters. It is shorter and more compact than 1 Timothy, and some of its gospel summaries are among the richest in the New Testament.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author (1:1) and was received by the church as his. It appears in the Muratorian list of the late second century, and early writers such as Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria quote it. The second-century teacher Marcion did not include it, or the other Pastoral Letters, in his collection of Paul's letters.

The authorship debate over the Pastoral Letters applies fully to Titus (see the introduction to 1 Timothy). Scholars who think a later follower of Paul wrote it point to vocabulary and style that differ from Paul's undisputed letters, to a church order with elders appointed in every town, to a false teaching they associate with a later period, and to the difficulty of fitting a mission on Crete into the story of Acts, which mentions Crete only as a place Paul sailed past as a prisoner (Acts 27:7-13). Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it answer that differences of style reflect a different kind of letter and subject; that appointing elders was Paul's practice from his first missionary trip (Acts 14:23); that the Jewish myths and quarrels about the law fit the first century; and that a mission on Crete fits the period after Paul's first Roman imprisonment, if he was released as early tradition reports. Mediating views suggest a secretary given freedom in wording or a later editor working with Paul's own notes. Evangelical scholarship generally holds to Paul's authorship; a majority of critical scholars do not.
date: If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from the same period as 1 Timothy, after his release from house arrest in Rome, around AD 62 to 64. Paul had evidently worked on Crete with Titus and left him there, and at the time of writing he planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis (3:12). A few scholars have tried to place the letter earlier, within the period covered by Acts, but the details fit awkwardly. Scholars who see the letter as written by a later follower of Paul usually date it between about AD 80 and 110.
setting:
Crete is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean, south of the Aegean Sea. It had been home to the Minoan civilization in the second millennium BC, and by the first century it was part of a Roman province that joined Crete with Cyrene on the North African coast. It had a substantial Jewish population, and Cretans were among those present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). The island also had a poor reputation in the Greek world for dishonesty and greed, which Paul acknowledges by quoting a Cretan poet traditionally identified as Epimenides (1:12).

Titus was a Gentile convert whom Paul had taken to Jerusalem and whom the apostles did not require to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3). He had served as Paul's representative to the troubled church in Corinth, where he handled difficult matters with success (2 Corinthians 7:6-15; 8:16-23). His task on Crete was to set in order what was unfinished (1:5), a young and loosely organized set of congregations in several towns, some of them unsettled by teachers who emphasized Jewish myths, genealogies, and quarrels about the law. Later Titus went to Dalmatia, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic (2 Timothy 4:10).
purpose: Paul writes to authorize and guide Titus in organizing the churches of Crete. He wants qualified elders appointed so that the churches can resist false teachers; he wants Titus to teach each group within the church how to live in a way that commends the gospel to outsiders; and he wants believers to devote themselves to good works, to be good citizens, and to avoid divisive controversy. The letter also carries practical arrangements: Titus is to join Paul at Nicopolis once a replacement arrives, and to help Zenas and Apollos on their way.
story: Titus belongs to the last stage of Paul's story, after the events recorded in Acts, when Paul was establishing leaders to carry on his work. Like 1 Timothy, it shows the transition from the apostolic founding of churches to their ongoing life under local leaders. In the New Testament it stands between 2 Timothy and Philemon, the last of the letters traditionally grouped under Paul's name before Hebrews.
christ: Titus calls both God and Jesus Christ Savior, sometimes in the same breath (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4-6), and it contains one of the New Testament's clearest statements of Christ's deity in most translations: the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13). Christ gave himself to redeem a people from lawlessness and to purify them for himself (2:14). Through him the Holy Spirit was poured out, so that those justified by grace become heirs of eternal life (3:6-7). The appearing of God's grace in Christ's first coming and the appearing of his glory at his return frame the whole Christian life.
reading: Read Titus as a companion to 1 Timothy and notice the differences as well as the likenesses: here the churches are younger, the instruction more basic, and the concern for outsiders' opinion very strong. Watch for the phrase good works, which recurs throughout, and for the purpose clauses that explain Paul's instructions, so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5) and so that believers will adorn the teaching about God (2:10). Some of the letter's instructions reflect household structures of the Roman world, and readers should consider how the principle underneath them applies today. Contested questions, especially about elders' qualifications, deserve a fair hearing of more than one view.

structure.title: Greeting
structure.summary: An unusually full opening in which Paul describes his apostleship in terms of the faith of God's elect and the hope of eternal life.

structure.title: Elders and false teachers
structure.summary: Titus is to appoint elders of proven character who hold to sound teaching, because rebellious teachers must be silenced and rebuked.

structure.title: Teaching for every household
structure.summary: Instructions for older and younger men and women, for Titus himself, and for slaves, grounded in the grace of God that trains believers to live godly lives as they await Christ's appearing.

structure.title: Good citizens saved by mercy
structure.summary: Believers are to be gentle and ready for good works toward all, because God saved them by his mercy through new birth and the Holy Spirit; they must avoid foolish controversies.

structure.title: Travel plans and greetings
structure.summary: Paul asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis, to help Zenas and Apollos, and to teach believers to meet pressing needs.

themes.title: Grace that trains
themes.body: The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and it instructs believers to renounce ungodliness and live upright lives (2:11-12). In Titus, grace is not only pardon but training. It saves and it shapes, and the two cannot be separated.

themes.title: Good works
themes.body: The phrase good works or good deeds, and related expressions, run through every chapter. False teachers are unfit for any good deed (1:16); Titus must model good works (2:7); Christ purified a people zealous for good deeds (2:14); believers must be ready for every good work (3:1) and devote themselves to meeting pressing needs (3:14). Good works do not earn salvation (3:5) but display it.

themes.title: The gospel and outsiders
themes.body: Paul repeatedly explains his instructions by their effect on those outside the church: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5), so that opponents will have nothing bad to say (2:8), so that slaves may adorn the teaching (2:10). Christian conduct in ordinary roles makes the gospel attractive or repellent to neighbors.

themes.title: God our Savior
themes.body: Titus uses the title Savior six times, three of God and three of Jesus Christ, often in close pairs. The letter's two great gospel summaries (2:11-14 and 3:4-7) describe salvation as the work of the Father's kindness, the Son's self-giving, and the Spirit's renewal.

themes.title: Sound teaching and leadership
themes.body: As in 1 Timothy, sound, healthy teaching is set against empty talk, myths, and quarrels. Elders must hold firmly to the faithful word so that they can encourage believers and refute those who contradict it (1:9).

keyChapters.why: Sets out the qualifications of elders on Crete and describes the false teachers they must resist.
Grounds instructions for every group in the church in the grace of God that trains believers, and names Jesus Christ our great God and Savior.
Contains one of the New Testament's fullest summaries of salvation by mercy through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
